title: The Letters in the Basement
logline: A forgotten basement archive of factory workers' letters reveals a 1934 strike that newspapers barely recorded, and a volunteer's sorting brings it back into history.

scenes.text: In 1969 a small town library opened its basement archive to the public for the first time.
scenes.summary: In 1969 a small town library opens its basement archive to the public for the first time.
scenes.rationale: Opening on the archive's first public opening sets the place and date that anchor the story.

scenes.text: Inside were more than 3,000 letters written by factory workers between 1920 and 1950. Most had never been read by anyone outside the families who donated them.
scenes.summary: The archive holds more than 3,000 letters by factory workers from 1920 to 1950, mostly unread outside the donor families.
scenes.search_query: handwritten factory worker letters 1920s 1940s archive boxes
scenes.rationale: The count and date range are specific claims best shown with the physical letters themselves.

scenes.text: A volunteer named Ayşe began sorting the letters by date.
scenes.summary: A volunteer named Ayşe begins sorting the letters by date.
scenes.search_query: Ayşe library volunteer sorting letters archive
scenes.rationale: Introducing the named volunteer needs a visual of her or her work so viewers can put a person to the discovery.

scenes.text: She noticed that dozens mentioned the same strike in the winter of 1934.
scenes.summary: Ayşe notices dozens of letters mention the same strike in the winter of 1934.
scenes.search_query: 1934 letter mentioning factory strike close-up handwriting
scenes.rationale: The pattern across letters is the central discovery and should be shown through the letters that mention the strike.

scenes.text: Newspapers from that year barely covered the strike.
scenes.summary: Newspapers from 1934 barely covered the strike.
scenes.search_query: 1934 local newspaper front page archive microfilm
scenes.rationale: Contrasting the scant press coverage with the letters needs period newspaper pages as evidence.

scenes.text: The letters describe it in detail: the closed gates, the shared meals, the slow return to work.
scenes.summary: The letters describe the strike in detail: closed gates, shared meals, the slow return to work.
scenes.search_query: 1930s factory gates closed strike workers shared meal archival photo
scenes.rationale: Archival imagery of factory gates and workers can illustrate the letters' descriptions while narration carries the detail.

scenes.text: Today the collection has been digitised, and historians use it to reconstruct a story the official record left out.
scenes.summary: The collection is now digitised, and historians use it to reconstruct a story the official record left out.
scenes.search_query: digitised letter collection online archive scan
scenes.rationale: Showing the digitised collection in use closes the arc from basement boxes to living historical source.

editorial_risks: The script does not name the town, library, factory or newspapers, so specific footage and documents will be hard to source and generic stand-ins could mislead viewers.
The claims of 1969 as the first public opening, more than 3,000 letters, the 1920–1950 range and dozens of strike mentions need sourcing from the library's records.
The claim that newspapers barely covered the strike needs verification through a review of 1934 local press.
Ayşe's identity, consent and any available photo of her need confirming; without one, use only her hands or the work, and label any reconstruction.
The 1934 strike details come only from the letters and should be framed as the workers' accounts, not independently verified facts.
Archival images of factory gates and strikes must be from the actual site or clearly labelled as illustrative to avoid implying they show this strike.
The claim about historians using the collection would benefit from a named historian or study, which the script does not provide.
